title: Sync vs Async Replication
description: Understand the spectrum of replication strategies — synchronous, asynchronous, and semi-synchronous — and their trade-offs between durability and performance.

segments.text: You know why we replicate data. Now let's talk about when replicas get updated. This timing decision — synchronous versus asynchronous — is one of the most consequential choices you'll make in a distributed system.

With synchronous replication, the leader waits for all replicas to confirm the write before telling the client it succeeded. The data is guaranteed to exist on multiple machines before the client gets an OK response.

The durability guarantee is strong. If the leader crashes one millisecond after confirming the write, the data survives on the replicas. Zero data loss. This is why financial systems and banking databases often use synchronous replication.

But there's a heavy cost. Every write must wait for the slowest replica. If one replica is across the ocean with 200 milliseconds of latency, every single write takes at least 200 milliseconds. Your write throughput is bottlenecked by network latency.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens to your system if one replica becomes unreachable? Can any writes succeed?

segments.text: Worse, if any replica goes down, writes are blocked entirely. The leader can't get confirmation, so it can't confirm to the client. Synchronous replication trades availability for durability. That's a direct CAP theorem trade-off.

Asynchronous replication is the opposite. The leader writes data locally, immediately confirms to the client, and replicates to followers in the background. The client doesn't wait for replicas at all.

Writes are blazing fast because they only hit one machine. Latency is measured in single-digit milliseconds. Throughput is limited only by the leader's capacity. This is why most web applications use async replication by default.

The risk? If the leader crashes before replicating a write, that data is gone. Vanished. The client thinks the write succeeded, but it didn't survive. This gap between acknowledged and replicated writes is called replication lag.
segments.thought_prompt: Is there a middle ground that gives you some durability without waiting for ALL replicas?

segments.text: Enter semi-synchronous replication. The leader waits for at least one replica to confirm, then responds to the client. The remaining replicas are updated asynchronously. You get durability on two machines without waiting for all of them.

MySQL uses semi-synchronous replication as an option. PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit setting gives you fine-grained control. Both let you tune the durability-performance trade-off per transaction if needed.

Think of it as a spectrum. Fully synchronous: maximum durability, minimum performance. Fully asynchronous: maximum performance, risk of data loss. Semi-synchronous: a practical middle ground. The right choice depends on what data loss your business can tolerate.

Next, we'll explore architectures where there is no single leader at all. Multi-leader and leaderless replication open up new possibilities, but also new challenges like conflict resolution. That's where things get really interesting.
